title: What Is JavaScript?
summary: JavaScript is the language that lets a web page respond when people click, type, and make choices.

subtopics.title: Instructions
subtopics.explanation: A program is a list of instructions the computer follows. `console.log("Hello")` asks the browser to write a message in its developer console. It is like giving a worker one clear step. The console is a learning and debugging tool, not a place visitors normally see page content. For example, a click handler can read a button action and update a message after a user submits a form. For example, open the console to inspect a message while the page itself remains unchanged.

subtopics.title: Values and names
subtopics.explanation: A value is information such as a number or a name. A variable gives that value a label so the program can use it later. `const city = "Pune"` stores text under the name `city`. It is like writing a name on a jar so you can refer to its contents. For example, a variable can keep the current score while a function calculates the next score. For example, a value can be stored in a variable and passed to a function.

subtopics.title: Decisions
subtopics.explanation: Programs can choose different actions based on a condition. `if (isRaining) { bringUmbrella(); }` runs an action only when the condition is true. It is like checking the weather before leaving home. Conditions let a program respond to changing information. For example, an if statement can show a different message when a required field is empty. For example, a condition selects a different path when the user has not filled a field.

subtopics.title: Functions
subtopics.explanation: A function is a named set of instructions you can run when needed. It is like a recipe: give it inputs and it follows steps. Functions help reuse behavior and make a program easier to read. A function can also return a result to its caller. For example, a function can format a price once and reuse that rule in several places. For example, an event listener connects a browser action to JavaScript behavior.

subtopics.title: Browser interaction
subtopics.explanation: The browser exposes tools JavaScript can use, such as reacting to clicks or reading form input. These tools are called Web APIs. It is like a toolbox supplied by the browser. JavaScript language features and browser APIs work together, but they are different parts of the platform. For example, a browser API such as fetch can request data, while JavaScript decides how to display the result. For example, keep server credentials out of client scripts because visitors can inspect them.

foundations.overview: JavaScript is a programming language that tells a browser or server what to do. It can update a page, respond to a click, or process data. Think of it like a set of instructions for a helpful assistant: values are the information, decisions choose a path, and functions group steps. Start with small changes and observe what the program does.
foundations.whyItMatters: JavaScript joins data, decisions, and actions into interactive behavior. Browser APIs expose page features, while the language itself supplies reusable programming tools.
commonUseCases: React to a user clicking a control.
Validate form input before submitting it.
Request information from a web service and update the page.

commonMisconceptions.myth: JavaScript is only used in web browsers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JavaScript also runs on servers and other environments, though available APIs differ.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Writing more code automatically makes a program more powerful.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Clear small steps are easier to understand, test, and change than unnecessary complexity.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The browser console is where visitors see page content.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Console messages are developer diagnostics; visible content belongs in the page interface.

visualExplorer.title: How the browser runs your JavaScript
visualExplorer.caption: Step through what happens from loading a page to executing and offloading async work.

config.intro: Follow a <script> from the moment the browser encounters it to how async callbacks run later.

steps.name: Parse the HTML
steps.detail: The browser reads the HTML top to bottom and finds a <script> tag referencing your JS.

steps.name: Hand code to the engine
steps.detail: The source is passed to the JavaScript engine (e.g., V8), which parses it into an abstract syntax tree.

steps.name: Interpret, then JIT-compile
steps.detail: The engine starts interpreting immediately and compiles hot code paths to optimized machine code.

steps.name: Run on the single thread
steps.detail: Statements execute one at a time on the call stack — only one thing runs at any moment.

steps.name: Offload async work
steps.detail: Timers, fetch, and events are handed to the runtime; their callbacks wait in a queue.

steps.name: Event loop drains the queue
steps.detail: When the stack is empty, the event loop runs queued callbacks, keeping the UI responsive.

interactiveExamples.title: Your first JavaScript output
interactiveExamples.explanation: console.log prints to the console — the most basic way to see JavaScript run. JS can also do math and join text with the + operator.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Hello, JavaScript! / 2 + 2 = 4 / JavaScript runs in browsers and Node.js

interactiveExamples.title: Dynamic typing in action
interactiveExamples.explanation: The same variable can hold a number, then a string, then a boolean. typeof reveals the current type — proof that types are decided at runtime, not declared up front.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: 100 number, then 'now a string' string, then true boolean.

interactiveExamples.title: Single-threaded but asynchronous
interactiveExamples.explanation: Even with a 0ms timeout, the setTimeout callback runs AFTER the synchronous code, because async work is queued and only runs once the call stack is clear.

codeLab.title: Detect the runtime
codeLab.instructions: Write a function describeEnvironment() that returns a short string describing where JavaScript is running. In this web sandbox, log a message and demonstrate using a value. Then log the type of the number 42 and a string to show dynamic typing.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A description string plus the types 'number' and 'string'.
hints: Use a return statement inside the function.
typeof gives the runtime type of any value as a string.

keyTakeaways: A program is a list of instructions the computer follows.
A value is information such as a number or a name.
Programs can choose different actions based on a condition.
A function is a named set of instructions you can run when needed.
The browser exposes tools JavaScript can use, such as reacting to clicks or reading form input.
